p: Joshua Chamberlain had been a professor of rhetoric at Bowdoin College before the war. He had taught himself tactics by reading military manuals at night. On the afternoon of July 2, 1863, he had already repulsed five Confederate assaults on the left flank of the entire Union Army.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: His regiment was nearly out of ammunition.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: The 15th Alabama, under Colonel William Oates, had been trying to turn the 20th Maine's refused left flank for nearly an hour. Each time, Chamberlain's men had stopped them. But the cartridge boxes were almost empty. The men were telling their officers they had nothing left to fire.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: Chamberlain had two choices: retreat, or attack. Retreat was unacceptable — his orders were to hold at all costs. Attack with empty rifles seemed suicidal. But Chamberlain understood something Oates did not: the Confederates below were as exhausted as the men above. The 15th Alabama had marched twenty-five miles that day before climbing and assaulting the hill. If he could shock them with an unexpected counter-charge, they might break before they understood what was happening.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: The command passed down the line. The 20th Maine — fewer than 200 men still standing in the ranks — fixed bayonets.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: The regiment swept downhill in a right-wheel motion, pivoting around the center and sweeping south and west. Chamberlain led from the front, a pistol in one hand and a saber in the other.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: Oates's men, climbing uphill toward what they expected to be a final assault on a shattered regiment, were instead hit by a wall of screaming men coming downhill at them.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: The 20th Maine captured nearly 400 prisoners. Chamberlain was slightly wounded — twice. He would receive the Medal of Honor for his actions on Little Round Top, presented thirty years after the battle. At the war's end, Ulysses Grant chose Chamberlain to receive the formal Confederate surrender at Appomattox.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: Lieutenant Colonel McGilvery rode up to Captain John Bigelow at a gallop.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Bigelow's Last Stand”, paragraph 1 of 10

p: 'I must have time,' McGilvery said. 'You must stay here and hold at any cost until I can form a new line.'

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Bigelow's Last Stand”, paragraph 2 of 10

p: Bigelow looked around. His battery — six Napoleon guns, nine horses each — was already under fire from Barksdale's Mississippi infantry advancing from the Peach Orchard. There was no infantry support anywhere nearby. McGilvery was asking him to hold a position unsupported against a brigade of Confederate infantry.
